o: Build target by appending words (each with a cost), minimizing total cost, or −1 if impossible. Example 1: "abc"(1) + "d"(1) + "ef"(5) = 7. Example 2: no word contains 'a', so −1. target up to 5*10⁴ and total word length up to 5*10⁴ demand a trie-backed DP rather than naive matching.
k: dp[i] = minimum cost to build target[:i]; dp[0] = 0, answer dp[n].
Store all words in a trie; from each position i, walk the trie along target characters — every trie node that terminates a word offers a transition i → i + depth with that word's minimal cost.
Total work is bounded by (number of start positions) × (trie depth along matched paths), efficient under the sum-length constraint.

a.i: Insert every word into a trie, keeping at each terminal node the cheapest cost among duplicate words. Then for each reachable dp[i], follow target[i:] through the trie; each terminal encountered relaxes dp[j+1]. This replaces repeated string comparisons with shared-prefix traversal.
s: Build a trie of words with min cost per terminal node.
For each i with dp[i] finite, walk target[i:] in the trie; at each terminal node update dp[pos+1] = min(dp[pos+1], dp[i] + cost).
a.t: O(total_word_length + n · D) where D is the deepest trie match from any position — fast under the sum-length ≤ 5·10⁴ constraint
a.sp: O(total_word_length) for the trie plus O(n) for dp

w: This is the standard accepted solution. An alternative groups words by length and compares rolling hashes of target substrings, guaranteeing O(L_distinct · n); mention it if asked about adversarial worst cases. Pitfalls: duplicate words (keep the min cost), unreachable prefixes (skip them), and returning −1 when dp[n] stays infinite. Follow-up: allow overlapping/reuse — the DP already allows unlimited reuse of each word.
